newsitem.title: POLAND: U.S. provided support for SFOR action in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. provided support for SFOR action in Bosnia.

text.p: U.S. peacekeeping troops in Bosnia provided logistical support for an operation on Thursday that led to the killing of a prominent Serb indicted for war crimes and the capture of another, U.S. officials said.

"U.S. SFOR (Stabilisation Force) forces provided some logistic and backup and transportation support to the operation. No U.S. forces participated in the detentions themselves, however," National Security Adviser Samuel Berger said in Poland during a visit by President Bill Clinton.

In the operation in a sector of Bosnia policed by British peacekeeping troops, Simo Drljaca, the former police chief of the northwest town of Prijedor, was shot dead after opening fire on SFOR soldiers, NATO announced in Sarajevo.

Another war crimes suspect, Milan Kovacevic, director of Prijedor hospital, was detained without incident and will be turned over to the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague for trial, said a statement issued at SFOR headquarters.
Berger refused to publicly discuss other details of the incident, which Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called "a very positive development".
But a White House official who asked not to be identified said Clinton had been briefed on planning for the operation last Saturday and gave his approval.

"We do not expect any (Serb) reaction, but if there was one, SFOR would react firmly to any reaction," the official said. He said Drljaca and Kovacevic were targeted because they were "coming into very frequent contact" with SFOR troops.
The official said the action had been carried out under the existing mandate of the NATO-led SFOR, which allows peacekeepers to arrest indicted war criminals if they come into contact with them.

"No indicted war criminal is exempt from the reach of those rules," he said. He declined to discuss why more high-profile suspects such as former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and military commander General Ratko Mladic, whose whereabouts have been known to NATO, had not so far been targeted.

Although the official said there had been no change in SFOR's rules of engagement, he said Thursday's action was in line with recent statements by Western leaders threatening a tougher line on indicted war criminals.
